blocks.robotComment: Same word, "learning" — three genuinely different processes underneath. 🧩
blocks.body: Machine learning splits into three broad paradigms, based on what kind of experience the system learns from: supervised learning (learning from labeled examples, where the right answer is already known), unsupervised learning (finding structure in data with no labels at all), and reinforcement learning (learning through trial and error, guided by rewards and penalties).

highlights.text: supervised learning
unsupervised learning
reinforcement learning

blocks.body: Supervised learning is the most common starting point: show the system thousands of emails already labeled 'spam' or 'not spam,' and it learns to predict the label on a brand-new email. The 'supervision' is the labels — someone already did the work of saying what the right answer looks like.

highlights.text: the labels

blocks.body: Unsupervised learning has no labels to lean on — instead it looks for patterns or groupings that exist in the data on their own, like automatically clustering customers into groups with similar buying habits, without anyone pre-labeling which customer belongs to which group.

highlights.text: looks for patterns or groupings that exist in the data on their own

blocks.body: Reinforcement learning is different from both: there's no fixed dataset of labeled examples at all. Instead, an agent takes actions in an environment, gets a reward or penalty based on the outcome, and gradually learns which actions tend to lead to better rewards — the same basic loop a game-playing AI or a robot learning to walk actually uses.

highlights.text: gets a reward or penalty based on the outcome

blocks.question: What distinguishes supervised learning from unsupervised learning?
options: Supervised learning uses labeled examples with known right answers; unsupervised learning finds structure with no labels at all
Supervised learning requires a human present at every prediction
Unsupervised learning only works on images
There is no real difference between the two
blocks.explanation: The presence or absence of labeled "right answers" in the training data is exactly what separates the two.

blocks.sentence: Learning through trial and error, guided by rewards and penalties for actions taken in an environment, is called ___.
options: reinforcement learning
supervised learning
unsupervised learning
blocks.explanation: Reinforcement learning is specifically defined by this reward/penalty feedback loop, not by labeled examples.

blocks.statement: Unsupervised learning relies on a dataset where every example already has the correct label attached.
blocks.explanation: That describes supervised learning — unsupervised learning specifically works without any labels at all.

lessons.title: How This Connects to What You Already Know

blocks.robotComment: You already know the umbrella. Now let's actually look inside it. ☂️
blocks.body: Machine learning is the middle layer of the AI/ML/deep-learning nesting: AI is the broadest goal (getting software to do things that normally need human intelligence), machine learning is one major approach to reaching it (learning patterns from data instead of hand-written rules), and deep learning is a specific kind of machine learning built on neural networks.

highlights.text: machine learning is one major approach to reaching it

blocks.body: This track goes deeper specifically into machine learning as a field: the different types of problems it solves, how a model actually gets evaluated, and the classic techniques that came before — and still sit alongside — the deep learning systems behind modern chatbots and image generators.

highlights.text: the classic techniques that came before — and still sit alongside — the deep learning systems

blocks.body: Not every machine learning system today is a deep learning system. Plenty of real, everyday ML — fraud detection, recommendation systems, medical risk scoring — runs on the kind of classic techniques this track covers, precisely because they're often simpler, faster, and easier to understand than a deep neural network, while working just as well for the specific problem at hand.

highlights.text: Not every machine learning system today is a deep learning system

blocks.question: How does machine learning fit into the broader AI/ML/deep-learning relationship?
options: Machine learning is one major approach to building AI; deep learning is one specific kind of machine learning
Machine learning is a synonym for deep learning
Machine learning is the broadest of the three terms
Deep learning came before machine learning existed
blocks.explanation: AI is the broadest goal, machine learning is one approach to it, and deep learning is one specific kind of machine learning within that approach.

blocks.sentence: Many real, everyday ML systems (like fraud detection) run on classic techniques rather than ___, because those techniques are often simpler and just as effective for the problem.
options: deep learning
unsupervised learning
reinforcement learning
blocks.explanation: Deep learning is powerful but not always necessary — plenty of practical ML uses classic techniques instead.

blocks.statement: Every machine learning system in real-world use today is built on deep learning specifically.
blocks.explanation: Deep learning is one kind of machine learning — many real systems use classic ML techniques instead, and work well doing so.

lessons.title: The Shape of an ML Problem

blocks.robotComment: Every ML problem, no matter how fancy it sounds, breaks down into the same three pieces. 🧱
blocks.body: Almost every machine learning problem has the same basic shape: an input (the information you start with), an output (the thing you're actually trying to predict or produce), and training examples — real, past input-output pairs the system learns the pattern from.

highlights.text: an input
an output
training examples

blocks.body: Take a spam filter: the input is the text of an email, the output is a label — "spam" or "not spam" — and the training examples are thousands of real emails that were already correctly labeled by someone in the past. The system never gets a rulebook for what makes an email spammy; it works that out from the pattern across all those labeled examples.

highlights.text: thousands of real emails that were already correctly labeled

blocks.body: This same input/output/examples shape holds up across wildly different problems: predicting a house's price (input: its features like size and location; output: a price; examples: past sale records), or recommending a video (input: what someone's watched before; output: a ranked list; examples: what people with similar history watched next). Once you can name these three parts, you can recognize an ML problem anywhere.

highlights.text: Once you can name these three parts, you can recognize an ML problem anywhere

blocks.question: In a spam filter, what plays the role of "training examples"?
options: Thousands of real emails that were already correctly labeled spam or not spam
A dictionary of banned words
The email server's configuration settings
A single perfect example email
blocks.explanation: Training examples are past, real input-output pairs — in this case, real emails already labeled correctly — that the system learns the pattern from.

blocks.sentence: The thing a machine learning system is actually trying to predict or produce is called the ___.
options: output
input
training set
blocks.explanation: The output is the target — the prediction or result the system is built to produce, like a spam/not-spam label.

blocks.statement: A machine learning system is typically given an explicit rulebook defining exactly what makes an email spam.
blocks.explanation: It isn't given explicit rules — it works out the pattern itself from labeled training examples.

quiz.title: Chapter Quiz — The Machine Learning Landscape

questions.question: What defines supervised learning?
options: Learning from labeled examples with known right answers
Learning purely through trial-and-error rewards
Finding structure in data with no labels at all
Memorizing a fixed rulebook written by a programmer

questions.statement: Unsupervised learning finds patterns or groupings in data without any labeled "right answers" to learn from.

questions.sentence: Learning through trial and error, guided by rewards and penalties, is called ___.
options: reinforcement learning
supervised learning
feature engineering

questions.question: How does machine learning relate to AI and deep learning?
options: Machine learning is one major approach to AI; deep learning is one specific kind of machine learning
Machine learning and deep learning are two names for the same thing
Machine learning is broader than AI itself
Deep learning came before machine learning existed as a field

questions.statement: Every machine learning system used in the real world today is a deep learning system.

questions.sentence: Real, past input-output pairs a machine learning system learns a pattern from are called ___.
options: training examples
output labels
hyperparameters

questions.question: In a spam filter, what is the "output"?
options: The spam / not-spam label the system predicts
The raw text of the email
The number of training examples used
The email server itself

questions.statement: The input/output/training-examples shape only applies to spam filters, not to other kinds of ML problems.

questions.sentence: Many real, everyday ML systems still run on classic techniques rather than ___, because those techniques are often simpler and just as effective.
options: deep learning
training data
labels

questions.question: Why is it useful to be able to name the input, output, and training examples of a problem?
options: It lets you recognize the shape of an ML problem in wildly different real-world situations
It has no practical use outside spam filters
It is only relevant for reinforcement learning specifically
It replaces the need for any training data at all

blocks.robotComment: Same 'labeled examples' idea from Level 1 — just two different shapes for the answer. 🎯
blocks.body: Supervised learning always starts from labeled examples, but the shape of the label itself splits it into two families: classification, where the output is one of a fixed set of categories, and regression, where the output is a continuous number.

highlights.text: classification, where the output is one of a fixed set of categories
regression, where the output is a continuous number

blocks.body: Think of email spam detection: every email gets sorted into one of two categories, 'spam' or 'not spam.' The set of possible answers is fixed and known ahead of time — the model is only ever choosing among those categories, never inventing a new one.

highlights.text: the model is only ever choosing among those categories, never inventing a new one

blocks.body: Now think of predicting a house's price: the output isn't one of a handful of pre-set choices, it's a number that could land almost anywhere — $210,000, $647,500, $1.2 million. That's regression: the target is a continuous number, not a category.

highlights.text: the target is a continuous number, not a category

blocks.body: A quick way to tell them apart: if you can list every possible right answer in advance, it's classification. If the right answer could be any value along a range, and listing them all doesn't make sense, it's regression. Predicting a customer's risk tier (low, medium, high) is classification; predicting their exact credit score is regression.

highlights.text: if you can list every possible right answer in advance, it's classification

blocks.question: Which of these is a classification problem?
options: Predicting whether a transaction is fraudulent or not fraudulent
Predicting the exact dollar amount of a transaction
Predicting how many minutes a delivery will take
Predicting tomorrow's temperature in degrees
blocks.explanation: Fraudulent vs. not-fraudulent is a fixed pair of categories — a classification task. The others are all continuous numeric predictions, which is regression.

blocks.sentence: A supervised learning task where the output is a continuous number, like a price or a temperature, is called ___.
options: regression
classification
clustering
blocks.explanation: Regression problems predict a number along a range, not a category from a fixed list.

blocks.statement: In a classification problem, the model can output a brand-new category that never appeared in the training examples.
blocks.explanation: A classification model can only choose among the fixed set of categories it was trained on — it can't invent a new one.

blocks.body: Classification isn't limited to two categories. Binary classification picks between exactly two options, like spam or not spam, but multi-class classification sorts an input into one of many possible categories — like tagging a photo as 'cat,' 'dog,' 'bird,' or 'other.'

highlights.text: Binary classification picks between exactly two options
multi-class classification sorts an input into one of many possible categories

blocks.body: Under the hood, most classifiers don't just blurt out one answer — they estimate how likely the input belongs to each category, then pick whichever category comes out most likely. A spam filter might be 92% confident an email is spam and 8% confident it isn't; it reports 'spam' because that's the stronger signal.

highlights.text: they estimate how likely the input belongs to each category, then pick whichever category comes out most likely

blocks.body: The stakes of choosing the right category list show up clearly in something like a medical scan triage tool, which might sort scans into 'urgent review needed,' 'routine follow-up,' or 'no action needed.' If that category list is missing an important case, the model has no way to express it — it can only pick from what it was given.

highlights.text: If that category list is missing an important case, the model has no way to express it

blocks.code:
Input: photo of an animal
Model's category options: cat, dog, bird, other
Model's confidence: cat 71%, dog 12%, bird 4%, other 13%
Predicted category: cat (highest confidence)
blocks.caption: How a multi-class classifier picks its final answer

blocks.question: A photo-tagging tool sorts every image into "landscape," "portrait," "food," or "other." What kind of task is this?
options: Multi-class classification, since there are more than two fixed categories
Regression, since there are four options
Reinforcement learning, since the tool is sorting images
Unsupervised learning, since photos are involved
blocks.explanation: Four fixed, known-in-advance categories is exactly multi-class classification — regression would require predicting a continuous number, not a category.

blocks.sentence: A classifier that estimates how likely an input belongs to each category, and returns the category with the highest likelihood, is choosing based on ___.
options: confidence
training examples
a reward signal
blocks.explanation: The model compares its confidence across all possible categories and returns the one it is most sure about.

blocks.statement: A classification model can only choose from the fixed list of categories it was trained on, even if the true answer falls outside that list.
blocks.explanation: This is a real limitation of classification: if the category list is incomplete, the model has no way to express an answer outside it.

blocks.body: Regression shares supervised learning's core setup — labeled training examples — but the output is a number along a continuous range rather than a category. That changes what 'correct' even means: a classifier is either right or wrong about the category, but a regression prediction can be closer or further from the true number.

highlights.text: the output is a number along a continuous range rather than a category
a regression prediction can be closer or further from the true number

blocks.body: Take a food delivery app predicting delivery time: the inputs might be distance, current traffic, and time of day, and the output is a number of minutes. If the true delivery took 34 minutes and the model predicted 31, that's a small, forgivable miss — nowhere near as bad as predicting 5 minutes or 90.

highlights.text: that's a small, forgivable miss

blocks.body: The same input/output/training-examples shape from Level 1 still applies: for house price prediction, the inputs are features like square footage, location, and number of bedrooms; the output is a predicted price; and the training examples are real past sales where the true final price is already known.

highlights.text: the training examples are real past sales where the true final price is already known

blocks.body: Some things can be framed either way depending on what you actually need: predicting a movie rating as 'exactly 7.3 out of 10' is regression, but predicting it as 'good, okay, or bad' is classification. The right framing depends on whether you need a precise number or just a useful bucket.

highlights.text: The right framing depends on whether you need a precise number or just a useful bucket

blocks.question: Why can a regression prediction be "closer" or "further" from the truth in a way a classification prediction cannot?
options: Because the output is a number along a range, so predictions can differ by small or large amounts
Because regression never uses training examples
Because classification always has more categories than regression has numbers
Because regression only works with images
blocks.explanation: A number has a notion of distance — 31 is close to 34. A category is either the exact match or it is not; there is no partial credit for the wrong category.

blocks.sentence: Predicting the exact number of minutes a delivery will take, based on distance, traffic, and time of day, is an example of ___.
options: regression
classification
unsupervised learning
blocks.explanation: The output is a continuous number of minutes, not a category from a fixed list — that is regression.

blocks.statement: The same real-world question can sometimes be framed as either a classification or a regression problem, depending on whether you need a precise number or a useful category.
blocks.explanation: Predicting an exact rating (7.3/10) is regression; bucketing it into good/okay/bad is classification — same underlying question, two valid framings.

questions.question: Which best describes a classification task?
options: Predicting one of a fixed set of categories for a given input
Predicting a continuous number for a given input
Learning through trial and error with rewards
Grouping data with no labels at all

questions.question: Which of these is a regression problem?
options: Predicting the exact temperature in degrees tomorrow
Sorting emails into spam or not spam
Tagging a photo as cat, dog, or bird
Deciding if a loan application is approved or denied

questions.statement: A classification model can output a category that never appeared in its training examples.

questions.sentence: A supervised learning task where the output is a number along a continuous range is called ___.
options: regression
classification
clustering

questions.question: What is multi-class classification?
options: Classification where the input can be sorted into more than two possible categories
A classification task that always fails
Regression applied to more than one number at once
Classification with no fixed category list

questions.statement: A regression prediction can be closer or further from the true value, unlike a classification prediction, which is simply right or wrong about the category.

questions.sentence: Most classifiers estimate how likely an input belongs to each category, then return the category with the highest ___.
options: confidence
penalty
label count

questions.question: Predicting a movie rating as "good, okay, or bad" instead of "7.3 out of 10" reframes the problem from regression into what?
options: Classification
Reinforcement learning
Unsupervised learning
It is not possible to reframe it this way

questions.statement: The same real-world question can sometimes be framed as either classification or regression, depending on whether a precise number or a useful category is needed.

questions.sentence: In a house-price prediction system, the price being predicted is the ___, and since it is a continuous number, this is a regression problem.
options: output
input
label list

lessons.title: Why You Can't Grade Your Own Homework

blocks.body: Imagine a student who gets the exact practice questions and answer key ahead of time, memorizes every answer word for word, and then takes a test made of those same exact questions. A perfect score wouldn't prove they understood the subject — it would only prove they can memorize. Evaluating a machine learning model on its own training data has the exact same flaw.

highlights.text: Evaluating a machine learning model on its own training data has the exact same flaw

blocks.body: If a model is tested using the very same labeled examples it was trained on, a model that simply memorized the quirks of those specific examples — instead of learning the actual underlying pattern — will score perfectly. That perfect score tells you nothing about how it handles a new input it has never seen before.

highlights.text: a model that simply memorized the quirks of those specific examples — instead of learning the actual underlying pattern — will score perfectly

blocks.robotComment: A perfect score on a rigged test is not a compliment. 🎓
blocks.body: This isn't just a technical nitpick. A model can score well throughout development and still perform badly the moment it meets real, new data — if every check along the way only ever used data it had already memorized.

highlights.text: if every check along the way only ever used data it had already memorized

blocks.question: Why is it misleading to evaluate a model using the same data it was trained on?
options: A model can score perfectly by memorizing the training data instead of learning a generalizable pattern
Training data is always too small to evaluate anything
Models are physically unable to process their own training data twice
It is not misleading — this is the correct way to evaluate a model
blocks.explanation: A model can look perfect on data it has already memorized while having learned nothing useful about new, unseen inputs.

blocks.sentence: A model that scores perfectly on its own training data but performs badly on new data has likely ___ the training examples rather than learning the general pattern.
options: memorized
generalized
ignored
blocks.explanation: Memorizing specific examples, instead of learning the underlying pattern, is exactly why training-data performance can be misleading.

blocks.statement: A model that scores perfectly when evaluated on its own training data is guaranteed to perform just as well on brand-new data.
blocks.explanation: A high score on training data alone doesn't prove anything about how the model handles data it has never seen.

lessons.title: Splitting the Data: Train and Test Sets

blocks.body: The fix for grading your own homework is simple in concept: before training even starts, split the labeled data into two separate sets — a training set, which the model actually learns from, and a test set, which is set aside completely untouched until evaluation.

highlights.text: a training set, which the model actually learns from
a test set, which is set aside completely untouched until evaluation

blocks.body: This only works if the separation is real: the test set has to represent questions the model genuinely never saw during training, not questions that snuck in some other way — otherwise you are right back to grading your own homework.

highlights.text: the test set has to represent questions the model genuinely never saw during training

blocks.body: Picture 1,000 labeled photos of cats and dogs. A common approach is training on 800 of them and holding the other 200 back entirely — the model never sees those 200 photos, or their labels, at any point while it's learning. Once training is done, those 200 photos are used, for the first and only time, to check how well the model actually performs.

highlights.text: the model never sees those 200 photos, or their labels, at any point while it's learning

blocks.robotComment: One peek at the answer key and the whole test stops meaning anything. 🔒
blocks.body: This rule is strict for a reason: even a small leak — like accidentally training on a handful of test examples — quietly inflates how good the model looks, without actually making it better. Keeping the test set untouched is one of the most basic disciplines in doing machine learning properly.

highlights.text: Keeping the test set untouched is one of the most basic disciplines in doing machine learning properly

blocks.question: What is the purpose of holding out a separate test set that the model never trains on?
options: To get an honest check of how the model performs on data it has genuinely never seen
To give the model more data to memorize
To make training faster
To replace the need for labeled data entirely
blocks.explanation: The test set only means something if it stays completely separate from training — that separation is what makes the evaluation honest.

blocks.sentence: Before training begins, labeled data is typically split into a training set and a separate ___ that the model never learns from.
options: test set
reward signal
category list
blocks.explanation: The test set is held back specifically so it can provide an honest, uncontaminated check of performance later.

blocks.statement: Accidentally including a few test examples in the training data has no real effect on how trustworthy the evaluation is.
blocks.explanation: Even a small leak between training and test data can quietly inflate performance scores without the model actually being better.

lessons.title: What a Test Set Actually Proves

blocks.body: Strong performance on a properly held-out test set is real evidence — it means the model is doing more than memorizing, because it's making good predictions on examples it genuinely never trained on. That's the entire point of keeping the split honest.

highlights.text: it means the model is doing more than memorizing, because it's making good predictions on examples it genuinely never trained on

blocks.body: What a test score doesn't prove is a guarantee for every possible future input. It's an estimate of real-world performance, and that estimate is only as trustworthy as how well the test set actually represents the situations the model will face later.

highlights.text: that estimate is only as trustworthy as how well the test set actually represents the situations the model will face later

blocks.body: Say a model is trained and tested entirely on daytime photos, and it scores very well. That high score says nothing about nighttime photos, because the test set never contained any — it can only honestly speak to the kind of data it actually included.

highlights.text: it can only honestly speak to the kind of data it actually included

blocks.robotComment: Foreshadowing: this 'generalization' idea is about to become the main character. 👀
blocks.body: A model that performs well on a good test set has cleared an important bar, but the deeper goal underneath all of this — performing well on genuinely new, real-world inputs in general, not just the ones in one particular test set — has its own name: generalization, and it's worth a much closer look.

highlights.text: performing well on genuinely new, real-world inputs in general

blocks.question: What does strong performance on a properly held-out test set actually demonstrate?
options: Real evidence the model learned a generalizable pattern, not just memorized training data
A mathematical guarantee of perfect future performance
That the model no longer needs any more data ever
That the training set was too small to be useful
blocks.explanation: A clean test score is meaningful evidence of real learning, but it is an estimate of future performance, not an ironclad guarantee.

blocks.sentence: A test score is only as trustworthy as how well the test set ___ the real situations the model will actually face.
options: represents
ignores
memorizes
blocks.explanation: If the test set does not represent real future conditions (like testing only on daytime photos), a good score can still be misleading.

blocks.statement: A model that scores well on a test set is guaranteed to perform well on every kind of input it might ever encounter in the real world.
blocks.explanation: A test score is a meaningful estimate, not a guarantee — it is only as representative as the test set itself.
